rv.q: Tenderness can be sweet or sore. Both are true for Ivy and Ash, the two young women who edge towards each other over the course of Eleanor Tindall’s surreal romcom thriller, Tender. Switching from naturalism to sudden psychological horror, the tonal shifts can feel awkward while the plot is crazily dependent on both tiny and huge coincidences.
At 90 minutes it is a meal, not quite filling enough but every morsel delicious.
Eleanor Tindall’s meet cute queer love story is appropriately moving, but comes with a lot of very distracting baggage.
Tender is tough-minded to its core – and terrific.

It’s a breathtaking dramatic experience, fuelled by an almost magical romance, unnerving tension, a creative team on song, and two leads who keep the Bush Theatre audience on tenderhooks almost the entire duration.

There is an awful lot in Tender, perhaps too much. The emotional intensity of the love story is always at risk of being lost amid the surreal body horror. But you will remember and root for Ivy and Ash, flawed as they are.
Tender is 1 hour 30 minutes of stellar acting with a script that leaves you aching for a little more.

Tender by name and tender by nature, it throws the kitchen sink and then some at an increasingly convoluted storyline, including self-harm, possible eating disorders and an apparent addiction to adult entertainment.

Having said that there's some excellent, quick-fire dialogue here, and even some laughs (although the gags around an abortion do fall a bit flat). Some of the lines are missed, alas, due to poor projection and staging. At times there is too much dialogue; a great deal of telling and not enough showing.
Tender is a confident and deeply engaging piece of new writing, elevated by two outstanding performances.

cn.t: This genre-bending queer romance-thriller earns mixed reviews for its ambitious tonal shifts and coincidence-heavy plot, though critics praise the beautiful performances and Tindall's sharp writing.
